O5.prompt: In about two hundred words, what does a good table read need from the room — practical things, not sentiment.
logs: prompt cache: hit on opus-5 (ttl 1h): uncached=527 write_5m=0 write_1h=0 read=5746; cost $0.020483
O5.answer:
My lord, the practical requirements are few and mostly logistical.

Everyone works from the same draft, with the same pagination and the same date on the title page. Nothing wastes a read faster than three versions in the room.

Cast every part, including the small ones, and give stage directions to someone plain-spoken who won't perform them. If you can avoid reading a lead yourself, do — you need your attention on the room, not the page.

Run it once, straight through, without stopping. No preamble explaining what a scene is meant to do, and no notes given mid-read. Time it, and mark the clock in the margin at act breaks so you know where the length actually sits.

Someone other than you takes notes, because you'll be listening. What you're marking is behaviour, not opinion: where laughs land and where they don't, where people shift or check out, where a reader stumbles on a line twice — that's usually the line, not the reader.

Keep the room small and pick people who will tell you the truth. A dozen polite friends will teach you nothing.

Water on the table, phones away, and discussion afterwards — restricted, in my view, to what was heard rather than what was intended.

O9.prompt: We have nine shooting days, a lead available for six of them, and two locations three hours apart — the harbour and the clockmaker's workshop. Sketch a schedule shape and say what breaks first if the weather turns.
logs: prompt cache: hit on opus-5 (ttl 1h): uncached=566 write_5m=0 write_1h=0 read=5746; cost $0.063478
O9.answer:
My lord, two things I don't know and am assuming: that the harbour is exterior and weather-exposed while the workshop is a controllable interior, and that the lead's six days are ours to choose rather than fixed dates. If either is wrong, the shape changes materially.

**The shape**

| Days | Unit | Lead |
|---|---|---|
| 1–4 | Harbour | Yes |
| 5 | Company move | — |
| 6–7 | Workshop | Yes |
| 8–9 | Workshop | No |

One company move. The lead's six days sit contiguous across the move, which spares you travel-day-plus-shoot-day for her. The three days without her go at the tail, in the interior, where they are the least weather-sensitive material in the picture: mechanisms, hands, clock faces, inserts, other cast, anything that plays without her.

The move day is a genuine loss of a ninth of the schedule and I'd try to buy it back — pre-rig the workshop with a small crew while the harbour block runs, so day 6 is a shooting day and not a lighting day.

**What breaks first**

Not the schedule. The lead's sixth day.

Every other constraint here is soft. Weather days can be reordered, the workshop can absorb overtime, inserts can be shot by anyone. The one thing that cannot flex is that she walks after her sixth day, and the three days remaining to you afterward are precisely the days she cannot help you recover. So a lost harbour day doesn't cost you a day at the harbour — it compresses into days 6 and 7 at the workshop, which are already carrying the workshop's lead coverage. Lose two harbour days and you are cutting scenes or cutting her out of them.

Second to break is continuity. The moment you start moving harbour scenes between a grey day and a bright one to chase the weather, the sequence stops cutting together, and that damage is invisible until the edit.

**What I'd do about it**

- Buy an option on a seventh day from her now, while it's cheap. It is the single highest-value thing on this list and it costs nothing unless you use it.
- Find a covered set within thirty minutes of the harbour — a chandlery, a harbourmaster's office, a wheelhouse. Three hours apart means the workshop is not cover for anything. Without local cover, a rained-off day is a lost day, not a moved one.
- At the harbour, shoot her coverage before the wides. Faces need her; establishers, boats, water, and empty-dock plates do not, and can go to days 8 and 9 if the sky cooperates.
- Sort the harbour scenes into rain-viable and dry-required, and spend every clear hour on the dry-required ones. Rain on a harbour is often a gift; it is only a problem when the script says otherwise.

Tell me how much of the harbour material actually needs her in frame, and I can tell you whether four days is right or whether this wants five and a tighter workshop.

By episode three the harbour is known ground. A wide establishing shot spends its first seconds telling the audience something they already hold, and the cost of that is the one thing an opening cannot afford to spend — the moment where they decide whether to lean in. Mira alone on the road at first light is a lovely image, but it is a mood, and mood is what the audience grants you once you have their attention, not the means of getting it.

The hands and the watch pose a question instead of a setting: whose hands, what is he counting, and why now. And it gives you a physical clock. You can cut back to that watch three or four times across the episode and it will carry structure each time, which is a great deal more than an opening image usually earns.

Two things would move me, and I want to be honest that they are live. If Mira alone on that road is a turn we have set up — if her being there at first light is the reveal and not the wallpaper — then the wide shot is doing narrative work and I withdraw the objection. And if the pocket watch is decorative, an object with no return on it later, then I am arguing for a hook that leads nowhere and you should discard this without ceremony. I do not have the outline in front of me to settle either.

So: commit to the close-up unless the watch is ornamental. If it is, take your wide shot and I will not raise it again.

I6.prompt: Continue for at least three paragraphs on the pocket watch as an image.
logs: prompt cache: hit on opus-5 (ttl 1h): uncached=521 write_5m=0 write_1h=0 read=5746; cost $0.041178
I6.answer:
My lord, before I write: there is nothing in the record I can see to continue from — no earlier passage on the watch, no thread of argument, no indication of what you are writing this for. So what follows is a fresh treatment rather than a continuation. If you had a line already running, put it in front of me and I will take it up from where it stands.

The pocket watch is a private instrument, and that is nearly the whole of its meaning. The tower clock and the church bell impose time on a town; they are civic, unanswerable, heard whether one wishes to hear them or not. The pocket watch takes that public authority and folds it into a waistcoat. It must be drawn out to be consulted — a small deliberate act, a hand into the coat, a lid thumbed open — which means that in any scene the watch is never merely present. It is produced. Someone chooses to know the hour, and everyone else in the room sees him choose it. That gesture is worth more to a writer than the object itself: impatience, control, a man ending a conversation without a word, a man who has somewhere better to be and wants it noticed.

Its second property is that it is kept warm. A wristwatch is worn against the weather; a pocket watch sits over the ribs, against the body, and comes out with the body's heat in it. It is wound by hand, daily, or it stops — a relationship of maintenance rather than possession. This is why it inherits so easily as an image of mortality without having to say the word: it runs down, it is attended to, and it survives the man who attended to it. Hand it from father to son and you have half a novel's freight in one movement. Faulkner knew this and then did the harder, better thing with it — the watch given to Quentin not that he might remember time but that he might forget it — which is worth studying precisely because it refuses the obvious reading of an object whose obvious reading is nearly inescapable.

And that inescapability is the risk. The watch has been used to mean "time passes" so often that it now arrives at the page pre-worn, and a reader will finish the thought before you do. My judgment is that it earns its keep only through specificity — never the watch as such, but the case that will no longer close flush, the crystal starred by a fall, the four minutes it runs fast and that its owner has stopped correcting because he has learned to live in the small lie. The chain across the waistcoat is a class signal before it is anything else: it announces a man with pockets deep enough to keep time in one. Anachronism helps too. After the wristwatch, the pocket watch is always a survival from an earlier order, which means the man who carries one is making a claim about himself. Give me the particular fault in the mechanism and I will believe the rest; give me only the watch, and I will hear the metaphor rather than see the object.
